draft.title: Writing dialogue
card: Good dialogue does two jobs at once. It shows what a character is like, and it moves the story forward.
People rarely say exactly what they mean. A character may dodge, change the subject or say something small while feeling something large.
The gap between what is said and what is meant is called subtext. The reader works it out from the words, the pauses and the context.
Dialogue that states every feeling outright, such as "I am angry and hurt", sounds flat and does not trust the reader.
draft.remember: Strong dialogue lets the reader hear the meaning beneath the words.

a.q: Which line of dialogue relies most on subtext to show a character's anger?
opts: "Nice of you to turn up," said Dad, not looking up
"I am furious that you were late," said Dad
"Your lateness makes me very upset," said Dad
"Tom, I feel disappointed that you were late"
a.why: Dad's words sound polite, but the reader senses his anger from the sarcasm and his refusal to look up. The other options name the feeling outright, so nothing is left for the reader to work out.
a.clue: Which character never names the feeling?

b.q: Zara's draft has two characters announce their feelings in full sentences. Which revision best improves the dialogue?
opts: Let them talk about something small while tension simmers
Add adverbs such as angrily and sadly after each line
Make each speech longer so every feeling is explained
Have a narrator explain what each speaker really meant
b.why: Talking about something small while feeling something large creates subtext, so the reader infers the feeling. Longer speeches and a narrator explaining each line state even more, which is the problem. Adverbs also tell the reader the feeling instead of letting the words show it.
b.clue: Look for the option that leaves the reader some work to do.

a.best: "Nice of you to turn up," said Dad, not looking up

b.best: Let them talk about something small while tension simmers
